plan.contextChunk: This figure combines a ray construction with an intensity curve for light passing through a single slit. At the left a vertical tan barrier is drawn in two segments with a narrow gap between them; a double-headed arrow spans the gap and a curved arrow connects it to the label a. A short teal arrow labeled lambda enters horizontally from the left and reaches the opening. From the slit five gray dashed lines fan out to the right toward a vertical gray line labeled Screen, and the middle dashed line runs straight along the horizontal. Two arcs measure angles from that horizontal reference: the outer upper line is marked theta_2 = 45 degrees and the inner upper line is marked theta_1 = ?, with two more dashed lines mirroring them below the axis. Drawn on the screen is a red wavy curve, tied by a curved arrow to the label Intensity on screen, whose sideways excursion represents brightness; it has a tall broad central peak on the axis and smaller lobes above and below, and each dashed ray meets the screen exactly where the curve pinches in to nothing. Lining the ray directions up with the nulls of the curve identifies each dashed line with a numbered diffraction minimum, so that the known 45 degree direction can be used to recover the slit width a and then the unknown angle theta_1.

interactionPlan.concept: Single-slit diffraction minima occur at angles satisfying a·sinθ = mλ, so the angular spacing of the pattern grows with wavelength and shrinks as the slit widens — and each dashed ray on the figure lands exactly at a zero of the screen's intensity curve.
elements: vertical tan barrier in two segments with a narrow central gap (the slit)
double-headed arrow spanning the gap, labeled a (slit width)
teal horizontal arrow entering from the left, labeled λ (wavelength)
vertical gray screen line on the right, labeled 'Screen'
horizontal dashed centerline from slit to screen
four symmetric gray dashed rays fanning from the slit to the screen (two above, two below the axis)
angle arc labeled θ₂ = 45° between centerline and outer upper ray
angle arc labeled θ₁ = ? between centerline and inner upper ray
red wavy intensity curve drawn along the screen, with a tall broad central peak and smaller side lobes
null points where the red curve pinches to zero, aligned with where each dashed ray meets the screen
curved arrow annotation labeling the red curve 'Intensity on screen'

interactions.label: Slit width a
interactions.teaches: Widening the slit compresses the diffraction pattern — the minimum angles and the nulls of the intensity curve move inward together, revealing the inverse relationship between slit width and angular spread

interactions.label: Wavelength λ
interactions.teaches: Longer wavelengths push every minimum and intensity null outward; shorter wavelengths pull them inward — making the proportionality sinθ = mλ/a directly visible on the screen

Selecting θ₁, θ₂, or a mirrored minimum highlights its dashed ray and the exact zero-intensity pinch point it reaches, showing that geometric ray directions and zeros of the intensity curve are the same condition: a·sinθ = mλ

demo_steps.title: Rays meet the nulls
demo_steps.narration: Each dashed ray from the slit meets the screen exactly where the red intensity curve pinches to zero. Click a minimum (θ₁ or θ₂) to see a ray and its null point highlighted together — the geometry and the intensity pattern are one condition: a·sinθ = mλ.

demo_steps.title: Narrow the slit
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slit-width slider downward: as the gap a shrinks, the dashed rays swing outward and the intensity lobes spread wider. A narrower slit diffracts light more strongly — the pattern expands.

demo_steps.title: Change the wavelength
demo_steps.narration: Now sweep λ: longer wavelengths push every minimum and null outward, shorter ones compress the pattern inward. With a known minimum like θ₂ = 45°, the relation a·sinθ = mλ lets you solve for a and then predict the unknown θ₁.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Every dashed ray lands precisely on a zero of the intensity curve because both are governed by a·sinθ = mλ — so shrinking a or lengthening λ spreads the whole pattern, and one known angle is enough to recover the slit width and every other minimum.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Left-to-right layout: tan two-segment barrier with a small central gap at left, teal λ arrow entering the gap, then a fan of five gray dashed rays (centerline plus two symmetric pairs) converging on a tall vertical gray screen at right. Angle arcs drawn at the slit between the centerline and the two upper rays, labeled θ₁ = ? (inner) and θ₂ = 45° (outer). The red intensity curve is drawn vertically along the screen with horizontal excursion encoding brightness: a dominant broad central peak centered on the axis, symmetric smaller lobes above and below, and pinch-to-zero points exactly where each dashed ray strikes the screen. Curved annotation arrows link 'a' to the gap arrow and 'Intensity on screen' to the red curve. As sliders change a or λ, rays, arcs, and the red curve must update coherently so rays always land on nulls; clicking a minimum highlights both its ray and its null point in a shared accent color.

authoredContext:
Calculating Single-Slit Diffraction Visible light of wavelength 550 nm falls on a single slit and produces its second diffraction minimum at an angle of 45.0° relative to the incident direction of the light, as in the figure. (a) What is the width of the slit? (b) At what angle is the first minimum produced?

In this example, we analyze a graph of the single-slit diffraction pattern.

Figure shows a vertical line on the left. This has a slit in the middle, of length a. A ray labeled lambda passes horizontally through the slit. This splits into 5 dotted lines that fall on a screen. The screen is shown as a vertical line. Of the five dotted lines, two make angles theta 1 and theta 2 with the horizontal. Theta 2 is 45 degrees. Theta 1 is smaller than theta 2 and is unknown. Intensity on the screen is shown as a vertical wave. The crest at the center, where a horizontal dotted line from the center of the slit falls on the screen, is the largest. The wave attenuates at the top and bottom. The remaining four dotted lines correspond to troughs in the wave.

Strategy From the given information, and assuming the screen is far away from the slit, we can use the equation asinθ=mλ first to find D, and again to find the angle for the first minimum θ1.

discrepancies: the source fixes θ₂ = 45°, but the generated figure computes it from a=2, λ=0.7 and labels it θ₂ = 44°, slightly off the canonical textbook values

the red intensity curve is sqrt-scaled so the side lobes are inflated and the central lobe dominates less dramatically than the source's tall multi-wiggle curve; at a glance the generated curve reads as one broad bump rather than the source's oscillating fringe profile
the dashed rays in the source extend past the screen region symmetrically above and below; the generated lower rays sprawl toward the bottom corners outside the screen line, cluttering the lower half
source 'Intensity on screen' annotation uses a curly brace-style arrow pointing at the curve; generated uses a thin arrow that nearly collides with the curve's lower tip
evaluation.notes: A faithful and pedagogically strong rendering of the single-slit diffraction figure — slit, λ arrow, dashed rays to exact nulls, screen, and intensity curve are all present with correct a·sinθ = mλ physics — undermined only slightly by the θ₂ = 44° (not 45°) default and the amplitude-rescaled intensity profile.
action_items: Pick default a and λ so that sinθ₂ = 2λ/a gives exactly 45° (e.g. a = 2√2·λ), so the figure matches the source's θ₂ = 45° while keeping the physics live
Reduce or remove the sqrt() amplitude scaling on the intensity curve (or scale side lobes less aggressively) so the central-lobe-dominant shape of the source is preserved while nulls stay exact
Clip or shorten the dashed rays so they terminate at the screen instead of sprawling past it toward the canvas corners

feedback.rationale: No failure modes, verification clean, concept and interactivity at 5/5 with a 4.4 average — the remaining discrepancies (θ₂ default of 44° vs 45°, sqrt amplitude scaling, ray clipping) are minor cosmetic polish that do not undermine the figure's correctness or usability, so further iteration is unlikely to yield meaningful improvement.
